notes.claim: LIRA is based on transmission line theory: it estimates and analyses the complex line impedance as a function of signal frequency, and measures the surge impedance over a wide range of frequencies.
Your notes say LIRA needs access to only one end, works on frequency-domain resonance effects of unmatched lines, and is sensitive to small changes in insulation permittivity.
Changes in dielectric permittivity change the cable impedance. A damaged segment differs mainly through a change in cable capacitance.

Joints, splices or defects create a deviation in the input impedance spectrum. The resonance frequencies give the cable length and the phase spectrum shows condition and locates joints and degradation.
Wirescan's patent gives the relative phase velocity from two consecutive resonance frequencies: vr = 2L(fk+1 − fk)/v0, where L is the length of the cable and v0 is the speed of light.
LIRA works with any termination except an exact match to the cable impedance, which makes the cable look endless.
DNORM indicates the severity of local impedance changes, and its sign helps determine the type of change.
DNORM normalises the spike difference from the terminal peak, and a local spot has a mirror image beyond the terminal peak from a second-order reflection.

Your notes give a negative DNORM for thermal degradation, water penetration and mechanical causes, and positive for bends and breaks in the shield. Colours run green mild, amber intermediate, red significant.
Your notes say tests are normally bi-directional, take about a minute each, run to 18 tests of core to screen and core to core, have no acceptance criteria, and need the raw trace data kept.
Wirescan's patent says LIRA can estimate the location of a degraded spot to within 0.5% of the cable length.
Both ends are earthed and discharged before a LIRA test so no energy is stored in the cable.
